warmup.q: fun totalGrams(crate: MutableList<Fruit>): Int only reads the list. You call it with apples: MutableList<Apple>. What happens?
options: It compiles: an Apple is a Fruit, so a crate of apples is a crate of fruit
It doesn't compile, and the only fix is to copy apples into a new MutableList<Fruit>
It doesn't compile, but MutableList<out Fruit> in the signature fixes it
It compiles, and fails at run time when totalGrams reads the first element
warmup.why: MutableList is invariant, because it both reads and writes E, so a MutableList<Apple> is not a MutableList<Fruit>. But totalGrams only reads, so it can ask for a take-only view: MutableList<out Fruit> accepts a crate of any subtype of Fruit. Copying works too, but you don't need it. Option one is the intuition that lesson 3 of this track disproved.

opening:
The shop's crates are the busy kind. All day, helpers take apples out and put apples in. That's why, in lesson 3, a crate of apples couldn't pass as a crate of fruit: someone might drop a lemon in.

Today one helper has a single job: weigh the apples in a crate and write down the total. They'll only take apples out, so the clerk at the door gives an instruction: "For this job, treat the crate as take-only." The helper, who has heard about the lemon, nods. The crate itself doesn't change, and the next helper may hear something else.

In code, MutableList is that busy crate. It reads and writes, so it can't be declared out or in, and a function that only reads still turns away a MutableList<Apple>. The easy trap is to copy the list, or cast it.

Contravariance with in: consumers ended with one in inside a parameter. In this lesson, we'll write take-only and drop-only views like that one and see what each allows. Then we'll line them up with Java's wildcards, and decide when to declare variance on the class instead. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a busy crate, and a helper told at the door, "for this job, take-only". A projection is that instruction. MutableList<out Fruit> lets one function take fruit out and put nothing in, and MutableList<in Apple> lets one function put apples in and read back only Any?. Java writes the same with ? extends and ? super.

Now look in your own code for a parameter typed MutableList<X>, or Java List<X>, that the function only reads. Each one turns away a crate of a subtype for no reason.

Next, we'll open the box whose label has worn off. What can you do with a list when you don't know its element type at all?

sections.h: A crate can't pick a side, so you project it for one job
sections.html:
Lessons 4 and 5 of this track put the variance on the class. Variance is the rule that decides whether a C<Apple> may stand in for a C<Fruit>, that is, whether it's a subtype. A Dispenser<out T> only hands values out, and a Bin<in T> only takes them in. Many types can't do that. MutableList<E> has get(): E and add(element: E), and Array<T> has get and set. T sits in both positions, so the class must stay invariant: a MutableList<Apple> is a MutableList<Fruit> only if Apple and Fruit are the same type. Lesson 3 showed what goes wrong when Java arrays pretend otherwise.

The trouble is that one function rarely uses both sides. Here is the copy example from the Kotlin docs, set in the shop. It puts the apples from one array into the shop window, an Array<Fruit> that holds two lemons. First, with no variance at all:

fun copyRow(from: Array<Fruit>, to: Array<Fruit>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] }

copyRow(apples, window)        // apples is an Array<Apple>
error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Array<Apple>', but 'Array<Fruit>' was expected.

Kotlin refuses for a good reason. If copyRow could see an Array<Apple> as an Array<Fruit>, it could write a lemon into it. But copyRow never writes to from. It only takes items out. So you tell the compiler that, right where the type is used, the way the clerk tells the helper at the door:

Java
// Java arrays are covariant, so a Fruit[] parameter already accepts an Apple[]
static void copyRow(Fruit[] from, Fruit[] to) {
    for (int i = 0; i < from.length; i++) to[i] = from[i];   // the JVM checks each store
}

copyRow(apples, window);           // fine
copyRow(apples, new Lemon[2]);     // compiles, then throws ArrayStoreException
Kotlin
fun copyRow(from: Array<out Fruit>, to: Array<Fruit>) {
    for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i]   // get() on Array<out Fruit> returns Fruit
}

copyRow(apples, window)                     // fine: Array<Apple> fits Array<out Fruit>
copyRow(apples, arrayOfNulls<Lemon>(2))     // compile error: Array<Lemon?> is not an Array<Fruit>

Array<out Fruit> is a type projection: an out or in written on one use of a type, instead of on its declaration. You haven't changed Array. You've asked for a narrower view of it, for one parameter: "an array of Fruit or of some subtype, which this function will only take items out of". Through that view, get returns Fruit, and set is gone:

from[0] = Lemon("Eureka", 95)
error: receiver type 'Array<out Fruit>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun set(index: Int, value: T): Unit'.

Writing variance where a type is used is called use-site variance. Java's wildcards, the ? in ? extends and ? super, are the same idea, and they are the only kind of variance Java has. Arrays are the odd case on the Java side. Java has no wildcards for arrays, because every Java array has been covariant since Java 1.0: an Apple[] passes as a Fruit[]. Instead, the JVM, the machine that runs the code, checks each store at run time. Java arrays never got the clerk's instruction. They got a guard. ArrayCopyDemoJava shows the guard at work: its second copy compiles, then prints ArrayStoreException: workbench.generics.l06.demo.Apple.

Kotlin's Array<out Fruit> compiles to a plain Fruit[], so the projection costs nothing at run time. The figure shows the three ways to look at one invariant type: the plain view takes out and puts in, the out-projection only takes out, and the in-projection only puts in.

Arrays are rare in everyday Kotlin. The same instruction on a MutableList is one you'll write often.

sections.h: Take-only: an out-projection is a read view, and Java spells it ? extends
sections.html:
Here is the helper's job from the opening: weigh any mutable crate of fruit. It only takes fruit out, so it asks for a take-only view:

Java
static int totalGrams(List<? extends Fruit> crate) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (Fruit f : crate) sum += f.getGrams();   // reads come out as Fruit
    return sum;
}

totalGrams(apples);    // a List<Apple>
totalGrams(lemons);    // a List<Lemon>
Kotlin
fun totalGrams(crate: MutableList<out Fruit>): Int {
    var sum = 0
    for (f in crate) sum += f.grams              // reads come out as Fruit
    return sum
}

totalGrams(apples)     // a MutableList<Apple>
totalGrams(lemons)     // a MutableList<Lemon>

ReadViewDemo prints apples: 330 g, lemons: 120 g.

Read MutableList<out Fruit> as "a mutable list of some subtype of Fruit, and I don't know which". That unknown is why putting anything in is forbidden. The list might be lemons, and adding a Gala would put an apple into a crate of lemons. So both compilers refuse every call that takes the element type:

crate.add(Apple("Gala", 180))
Kotlin: receiver type 'MutableList<out Fruit>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'.
Java:   incompatible types: Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1

Even a perfectly good apple is turned away, from a crate that really holds apples. The clerk isn't being rude. Through a take-only view, nobody can tell a crate of apples from a crate of lemons. CAP#1 is the name that javac, the Java compiler, gives that unknown: a captured type, a placeholder for "the one real element type of this particular list". Kotlin prints it as CapturedType(out Fruit), for example when you try val a: Apple = crate[0]. Nothing you can write is known to be a subtype of the placeholder, so nothing goes in.

Here the picture of the clerk's instruction breaks. A helper told "take-only" wouldn't tip the crate out on the floor, but a take-only view allows it. Members that don't take an element still work: size, isEmpty(), removeAt(0) and clear() all compile through the view, as lesson 4 showed. The demo removes the Gala through a view and prints after removeAt through the view: [Fuji]. A projection limits which types flow in. It doesn't stop the crate from changing.

You need this only for invariant types. Kotlin's read-only List, the glass display case of lesson 3, is already declared List<out E>. So a plain List<Fruit> parameter accepts a List<Apple>. Write List<out Fruit> anyway, and the compiler warns that the projection is redundant. You'll see that warning in the Try-it.

A function that only takes items out of a crate should say so. Write MutableList<out T>, or take a plain List.

Take-only is one instruction. The clerk has a second one, for helpers who only put things in.

steps: Run ReadViewDemo (or ReadViewDemoJava). One function weighs a crate of apples and a crate of lemons.
Uncomment the two wrong moves one at a time, predict, run.
Change totalGrams's parameter to a read-only List<Fruit> and run. Then change it to List<out Fruit>, and look for a w: line in the build output.

code.title: ReadViewDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l06.demo /** Weighs any mutable crate of fruit. It only takes fruit out, so it asks for an out-projection. */ fun totalGrams(crate: MutableList<out Fruit>): Int { var sum = 0 for (f in crate) sum += f.grams // reads come out as Fruit // crate.add(Apple("Gala", 180)) // wrong move 1: no add() through an out-projection return sum } fun main() { val apples: MutableList<Apple> = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) val lemons: MutableList<Lemon> = mutableListOf(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) println("apples: ${totalGrams(apples)} g, lemons: ${totalGrams(lemons)} g") val view: MutableList<out Fruit> = apples // the same projection on a variable view.removeAt(0) // still allowed: removeAt takes an Int, not a T println("after removeAt through the view: $apples") // Wrong move 2: no projection, so a MutableList<Apple> is not a MutableList<Fruit>. // val strict: MutableList<Fruit> = apples }

alt.title: ReadViewDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ReadViewDemo.kt. ? extends at the use site is Kotlin's out-projection. */ public class ReadViewDemoJava { static int totalGrams(List<? extends Fruit> crate) { int sum = 0; for (Fruit f : crate) sum += f.getGrams(); // reads come out as Fruit // crate.add(new Apple("Gala", 180)); // wrong move 1: no add() through ? extends return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<Lemon> lemons = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 120))); System.out.println("apples: " + totalGrams(apples) + " g, lemons: " + totalGrams(lemons) + " g"); List<? extends Fruit> view = apples; // the same wildcard on a variable view.remove(0); // still allowed: remove(int) takes no T System.out.println("after remove through the view: " + apples); // Wrong move 2: no wildcard, so a List<Apple> is not a List<Fruit>. // List<Fruit> strict = apples; } }

try.expect: Both print apples: 330 g, lemons: 120 g and then [Fuji]: removeAt (Java: remove(int)) worked through the read view. add fails with Receiver type 'MutableList<out Fruit>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. (Java: incompatible types: Apple cannot be converted to CAP#1), and the strict assignment with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'MutableList<Fruit>', actual 'MutableList<Apple>'. (Java: List<Apple> cannot be converted to List<Fruit>). List<Fruit> compiles with no projection. List<out Fruit> compiles with the warning Projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out Fruit>' has the same variance.

sections.h: Drop-only: an in-projection is a write view, and Java spells it ? super
sections.html:
Now flip the direction. This helper tops up a crate with Gala apples, and only ever puts apples in:

Java
static void restock(List<? super Apple> crate, int count) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) crate.add(new Apple("Gala", 180));
}

restock(apples, 1);      // a List<Apple>
restock(fruit, 2);       // a List<Fruit>
restock(anything, 2);    // a List<Object>
Kotlin
fun restock(crate: MutableList<in Apple>, count: Int) {
    repeat(count) { crate.add(Apple("Gala", 180)) }
}

restock(apples, 1)       // a MutableList<Apple>
restock(fruit, 2)        // a MutableList<Fruit>
restock(anything, 2)     // a MutableList<Any>

MutableList<in Apple> means "a mutable list of Apple, or of a type above Apple such as Fruit or Any". Every such list accepts an apple, so add is safe. WriteViewDemo prints apples = [Fuji, Gala], fruit = [Eureka, Gala, Gala], anything = [a paper bag, Gala, Gala].

Taking things out is the side that gets weaker. The first item might be the Fuji, the Eureka lemon or the paper bag that was already there, and the demo prints all three. So the only thing the compiler can promise about a read is Any? (in Java, Object):

val firstApple: Apple = crate[0]
Kotlin: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Apple', actual 'CapturedType(in Apple)'.
Java:   incompatible types: CAP#1 cannot be converted to Apple

A MutableList<Lemon> is turned away at the call, because a crate of lemons can't take an apple: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Lemon>', but 'MutableList<in Apple>' was expected.

The JDK, Java's standard library, writes its utility methods this way, and calling them from Kotlin is a good way to learn the mapping. Here are two of them from java.util.Collections, with the same contracts written in Kotlin:

Java
public static <T> void fill(List<? super T> list, T obj) { /* ... */ }
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) { /* ... */ }
Kotlin
fun <T> fill(list: MutableList<in T>, obj: T) { /* ... */ }
fun <T> copy(dest: MutableList<in T>, src: List<T>) { /* ... */ }

Pass the wrong thing to the real Collections.copy from Kotlin, and the error shows how Kotlin reads Java's wildcards:

java.util.Collections.copy(apples, listOf("Gala"))
error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'List<String>', but '(Mutable)List<out Apple!>!' was expected.

Java's ? extends became out. The rule in the Kotlin docs is that Foo<? extends Bar> becomes Foo<out Bar!>!, and Foo<? super Bar> becomes Foo<in Bar!>!. The ! marks a platform type, a type from Java whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know. (Mutable)List means Kotlin can't tell whether Java will change the list. The mapping works the other way too: a Kotlin parameter MutableList<in T> compiles to Java's List<? super T>, and this lesson's lab checks exactly that.

So there are two places to write out and in: on the class, or on one use of it. Which one should you reach for?

It only puts apples in, so any crate that takes apples will do. */ fun restock(crate: MutableList<in Apple>, count: Int) { repeat(count) { crate.add(Apple("Gala", 180)) } // putting an Apple in: fine val first: Any? = crate.firstOrNull() // reading compiles, but all you get is Any? println(" first is $first") // val firstApple: Apple = crate[0] // wrong move 1: an in-projection can't promise an Apple } fun main() { val apples = mutableListOf(Apple("Fuji", 150)) val fruit = mutableListOf<Fruit>(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) val anything = mutableListOf<Any>("a paper bag") restock(apples, 1) restock(fruit, 2) restock(anything, 2) println("apples = $apples, fruit = $fruit, anything = $anything") java.util.Collections.fill(fruit, Apple("Fuji", 150)) // the JDK's fill(List<? super T> list, T obj) println("after Collections.fill: $fruit") // Wrong move 2: a crate of lemons can't take an apple. val lemons: MutableList<Lemon> = mutableListOf(Lemon("Eureka", 95)) // restock(lemons, 1) }

alt.html: package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of WriteViewDemo.kt. ? super at the use site is Kotlin's in-projection. */ public class WriteViewDemoJava { static void restock(List<? super Apple> crate, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) crate.add(new Apple("Gala", 180)); // putting an Apple in: fine Object first = crate.isEmpty() ? null : crate.get(0); // reading compiles, as Object System.out.println(" first is " + first); // Apple firstApple = crate.get(0); // wrong move 1: ? super can't promise an Apple } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<Fruit> fruit = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 120))); List<Object> anything = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a paper bag")); restock(apples, 1); restock(fruit, 2); restock(anything, 2); System.out.println("apples = " + apples + ", fruit = " + fruit + ", anything = " + anything); Collections.fill(fruit, new Apple("Fuji", 150)); // fill(List<? super T> list, T obj) System.out.println("after Collections.fill: " + fruit); // Wrong move 2: a crate of lemons can't take an apple. // restock(new ArrayList<Lemon>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 95))), 1); } }

Wrong move 2: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Lemon>', but 'MutableList<in Apple>' was expected. (Java: ArrayList<Lemon> cannot be converted to List<? super Apple>). sections.h: Declare variance once when you can, project when you must
sections.html:
The rule for choosing is short.

If every public member of a class only hands T out, declare out T on the class. If every member only takes T in, declare in T. You do it once, and every caller benefits: nobody writes a projection, and a List<Apple> simply is a List<Fruit>. This is declaration-site variance, and it's why Kotlin code has far fewer wildcards than Java code.

If the class both takes and gives T, it stays invariant. MutableList and Array are like that, and so is any crate, cache or store with a put and a get. Then each function that uses only one side asks for a projection. Here is a crate class of our own, with one function of each kind:

Java
static final class Crate<T> {                  // takes and gives T: invariant
    private final List<T> items = new ArrayList<>();
    void put(T item) { items.add(item); }
    T top() { return items.get(items.size() - 1); }
}

static String topName(Crate<? extends Fruit> crate) { return crate.top().getName(); }
static void putApple(Crate<? super Apple> crate, String name, int grams) {
    crate.put(new Apple(name, grams));
}
Kotlin
class Crate<T> {                               // takes and gives T: invariant
    private val items = mutableListOf<T>()
    fun put(item: T) { items += item }
    fun top(): T = items.last()
}

fun topName(crate: Crate<out Fruit>): String = crate.top().name
fun putApple(crate: Crate<in Apple>, name: String, grams: Int) =
    crate.put(Apple(name, grams))

ChooseDemo puts a Gala into a crate of apples and a Fuji into a mixed crate that holds a lemon, and prints Gala Fuji. The plain types still don't mix: val strict: Crate<Fruit> = apples fails, because the projections live on the two functions, not on the class.

Java has no declaration-site variance, so every Java class works like Crate. Each method that only reads or only writes must remember its wildcard, and the JDK has hundreds of them. Forget one, and your own tests still pass. The first caller with a List<Apple> finds out.

The Kotlin compiler also guards the line between the two kinds of variance:

You write The compiler says
List<out Fruit> warning: projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out Fruit>' has the same variance.
List<in Fruit> error: projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in Fruit>'. Remove the projection or replace it with '*'.
fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) error: variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces.

The last one catches people. Variance says when a C<A> can stand in for a C<B>. A generic function is not a type that one thing can stand in for, so out on its own type parameter has nothing to describe. Put the projection on a parameter's type instead, as copyInto does in this lesson's lab.

Declare variance on the class when every member uses one side. Project at the use site when the class uses both.

A projection still names a type, though: out Fruit, in Apple. The '*' in the second message is for the case where you can't name one at all, a crate whose label has worn off. That's the next lesson.

try.title: Take from one crate, put into another
steps: Run ChooseDemo (or ChooseDemoJava). topName only takes from a crate; putApple only puts into one.
Uncomment the wrong move in main, predict, run.
At the bottom of ChooseDemo.kt, predict which of lines 1 to 3 is a warning and which are errors. Uncomment them one at a time to check.

code.title: ChooseDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l06.demo /** Takes T in AND hands T out, so it can't be declared out or in. It stays invariant. */ class Crate<T> { private val items = mutableListOf<T>() fun put(item: T) { items += item } fun top(): T = items.last() } // Only takes out: ask for a take-only view. A Crate<Apple> fits. fun topName(crate: Crate<out Fruit>): String = crate.top().name // Only puts apples in: ask for a drop-only view. A Crate<Fruit> fits. fun putApple(crate: Crate<in Apple>, name: String, grams: Int) = crate.put(Apple(name, grams)) fun main() { val apples = Crate<Apple>() val mixed = Crate<Fruit>() mixed.put(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) putApple(apples, "Gala", 180) putApple(mixed, "Fuji", 150) println("${topName(apples)} ${topName(mixed)}") // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // val strict: Crate<Fruit> = apples } // Predict each line, then uncomment it alone and run. // fun redundant(fruit: List<out Fruit>) {} // 1 // fun conflicting(fruit: List<in Fruit>) {} // 2 // fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) {} // 3

alt.title: ChooseDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ChooseDemo.kt. Java has only use-site variance, so every class is like Crate: * invariant, with ? extends or ? super written by each method that only reads or only writes. */ public class ChooseDemoJava { static final class Crate<T> { private final List<T> items = new ArrayList<>(); void put(T item) { items.add(item); } T top() { return items.get(items.size() - 1); } } // only takes out: ? extends static String topName(Crate<? extends Fruit> crate) { return crate.top().getName(); } // only puts apples in: ? super static void putApple(Crate<? super Apple> crate, String name, int grams) { crate.put(new Apple(name, grams)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Crate<Apple> apples = new Crate<>(); Crate<Fruit> mixed = new Crate<>(); mixed.put(new Lemon("Eureka", 120)); putApple(apples, "Gala", 180); putApple(mixed, "Fuji", 150); System.out.println(topName(apples) + " " + topName(mixed)); // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // Crate<Fruit> strict = apples; } }

try.expect: Both print Gala Fuji. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Crate<Fruit>', actual 'Crate<Apple>'. (Java: Crate<Apple> cannot be converted to Crate<Fruit>): the projections are on the functions, not on the class. Line 1 compiles with the Projection is redundant warning. Line 2 fails with Projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in Fruit>'. Line 3 fails with Variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces.

compare.title: The same copy and fill contracts with wildcards and with projections

java.title: Transfers.java
java.html: import java.util.List; final class Transfers { // dest only takes T, src only gives T: the shape of Collections.copy static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); return from.size(); } // only writes: ? super static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(value); } // a read-only parameter still needs ? extends in Java static double sumAll(List<? extends Number> amounts) { double sum = 0; for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue(); return sum; } }

kotlin.title: Projections.kt
kotlin.html: // MutableList is invariant, so each function projects it at the use site fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>): Int { for (x in from) to.add(x) return from.size } fun <T> fillWith(target: MutableList<in T>, value: T, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(value) } } // List is declared List<out E>: no projection needed (one would only earn a warning) fun sumAll(amounts: List<Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() return sum }

compare.note: For MutableList, the two versions say exactly the same thing. Kotlin's MutableList<out T> compiles to Java's List<? extends T>, MutableList<in T> compiles to List<? super T>, and Kotlin shows Java's wildcards back to you as out and in. The real difference is sumAll. Java has no read-only list type with declared variance, so every reading parameter needs ? extends. Kotlin's List carries out E on its declaration, so the plain type is already flexible, and a projection on it is redundant. Arrays differ too: Java arrays are covariant, with a run-time check on every store and no wildcards, while Kotlin's Array<out T> is a compile-time projection that compiles down to a plain Java array.

worked.title: Unpack the delivery crate onto the shop floor

steps.say: The morning delivery comes in a crate of apples. A helper moves every apple onto the shop floor, adds up the weight, and empties the delivery crate. The first draft uses plain types. The shop floor is a MutableList<Fruit>, because it also holds lemons. Read the error.
steps.code: fun unpack(delivery: MutableList<Apple>, floor: MutableList<Apple>): Int { var grams = 0 for (a in delivery) { floor.add(a); grams += a.grams } delivery.clear() return grams } val delivery = mutableListOf(Apple("Gala", 180), Apple("Fuji", 150)) val floor = mutableListOf<Fruit>(Lemon("Eureka", 120)) unpack(delivery, floor) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Fruit>', // but 'MutableList<Apple>' was expected.

alt.html: static int unpack(List<Apple> delivery, List<Apple> floor) { int grams = 0; for (Apple a : delivery) { floor.add(a); grams += a.grams(); } delivery.clear(); return grams; } List<Apple> delivery = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Apple("Gala", 180), new Apple("Fuji", 150))); List<Fruit> floor = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Lemon("Eureka", 120))); unpack(delivery, floor); // error: incompatible types: List<Fruit> cannot be converted to List<Apple>

steps.say: Name what each parameter does with apples. delivery gives them to you, and is cleared at the end, which takes no element. floor only receives them. So for this one function, delivery is a producer and floor is a consumer. Both are MutableList, which can't be declared out or in, so the variance goes on the parameters.
Project each parameter. Self-check before reading the comments: why does delivery.clear() still compile through an out-projection? (It takes no element, so it can't let a wrong type in.)
steps.code: fun unpack(delivery: MutableList<out Apple>, floor: MutableList<in Apple>): Int { var grams = 0 for (a in delivery) { // 1. take out: each a is an Apple floor.add(a) // 2. put in: the floor takes Apple or anything above it grams += a.grams } delivery.clear() // 3. no element in clear(), so the take-only view allows it return grams } unpack(delivery, floor) // compiles: 330, and the floor holds the lemon and both apples

alt.html: static int unpack(List<? extends Apple> delivery, List<? super Apple> floor) { int grams = 0; for (Apple a : delivery) { // 1. take out: producer extends floor.add(a); // 2. put in: consumer super grams += a.grams(); } delivery.clear(); // 3. no T in clear() return grams; } unpack(delivery, floor); // compiles

steps.say: Check it from the caller's side. The floor can now be a MutableList<Apple>, a MutableList<Fruit> or a MutableList<Any>. If you later need unpack to read back from the floor (say, to skip a variety that's already on display), that read returns Any? through the in-projection, and the compiler tells you so. At that point the parameter really is read and write, and it should go back to the plain type.

lab.title: Project MutableList at the use site, then do it in Java
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. The signature tests print what Java sees today, such as but was: "List<T>": no projection means no wildcard.
In Projections.kt, give copyInto's from an out and its to an in, then write the loop and return the count. The tests copy a MutableList<Int> into a MutableList<Number>.
Give fillWith's target the projection that matches "only written", then append count copies.
Write sumAll. Then change its parameter to List<out Number>, run the tests, and find the warning in the output. Put the plain List<Number> back.
In Transfers.java, change drainTo's parameters to Queue<? extends T> and Collection<? super T>, then take items from the queue until it is empty.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: for (x in from) to.add(x) type-checks because a read from MutableList<out T> gives a T, and MutableList<in T> accepts a T.
Queue.poll() returns null when the queue is empty: for (T item = from.poll(); item != null; item = from.poll()).
Why does sumAll(ints) compile before you touch it? Because Kotlin's List is declared List<out E>. Only MutableList needs the projection.

drill.title: Write copyInto and its Java signature from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write copyInto(from, to) for two MutableLists in Kotlin, with the projections that let a MutableList<Apple> be copied into a MutableList<Fruit>. Then write the Java method that Kotlin generates for it (the signature is enough), and the Java version of fillWith.

answer.html: fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>): Int { for (x in from) to.add(x) // reads give T, writes take T return from.size } fun <T> fillWith(target: MutableList<in T>, value: T, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(value) } } // Java sees: public static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) // public static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count)

alt.title: Transfers.java
alt.html: static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); // producer extends, consumer super return from.size(); } static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(value); }

recap: A type that both takes and gives T (MutableList, Array, your own Crate) must stay invariant.
A type projection adds out or in at one use: MutableList<out Fruit> is a take-only view, and MutableList<in Apple> is a drop-only view.
Through an out-projection, reads give the bound and calls that take T are refused. Through an in-projection, T values go in and reads give only Any?.
Kotlin's out T and in T projections compile to Java's ? extends T and ? super T, and Java's wildcards show up in Kotlin as out and in.

Declare variance on the class when every member uses one side, and project at the use site when the class uses both. Projecting an already-variant type earns a warning (List<out T>) or an error (List<in T>).
The limit: a projection still names a type (out Fruit, in Apple). For a list whose element type you don't know at all, you need the star projection.

explain.prompt: A teammate's fun totalGrams(crate: MutableList<Fruit>) rejects their MutableList<Apple>. They propose making MutableList covariant "like List". Explain why that can't work, and what to write instead.
explain.answer: MutableList has add(element: E) as well as get(): E, so E sits in an in-position and an out-position. If a MutableList<Apple> could be used as a MutableList<Fruit>, someone could add a lemon to a crate of apples, which is exactly the bug Java arrays have. So the class has to stay invariant. But totalGrams only reads, so it can ask for a take-only view in its own signature: MutableList<out Fruit>. That accepts a crate of any subtype of Fruit, gives back Fruit on reads, and refuses add. Even simpler, if totalGrams never changes the list, it can take a plain read-only List<Fruit>, which is already covariant. In Java, the same parameter is List<? extends Fruit>.

deeper.html:
Both compilers turn a wildcard or projection into a fresh captured type each time they check an expression: "the one specific type this list really has". That's why CAP#1 shows up in javac messages. Java can also capture a wildcard for a method call, which gives a well-known trick. You can't write l.set(i, l.get(j)) on a List<?>, but you can pass the List<?> to a private generic helper <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l, int i, int j), and inside the helper the element type has a name. The JDK chose not to bother. Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) assigns the list to a raw List and calls l.set(i, l.set(j, l.get(i))) under @SuppressWarnings, with a source comment saying that capturing the wildcard would need a supplementary private method.

Kotlin captures projected arguments for calls too. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the calls swap(star, 0, 1) with star: MutableList<*> and swap(view, 0, 1) with view: MutableList<out Fruit> both compile with kotlinc 2.4.21. Inside swap, T is the captured type, so values read from the list may be written back into the same list. You'll meet MutableList<*> properly in the next lesson.

Arrays have one more twist. Because Java arrays carry no wildcards, Kotlin compiles Array<out Fruit> and Array<Fruit> both to Fruit[], and Array<in Fruit> to Object[]. From Java, those differences are invisible; the projection exists only for the Kotlin compiler. The door opens the other way too. Kotlin shows a Java Object[] parameter as Array<(out) Any!>!, so you may pass an Array<String> to it, as Java code could. That brings Java's covariance back: java.util.Arrays.fill(names, 42) with names: Array<String> compiles in Kotlin and throws ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at run time.
